chapter: Jelly Roll, Leonard Reed and Chicago mixed crowds
title: White musicians at the Golden Lily breakfast dances; June Richmond
summary: He recalls white musicians and stars visiting, and a singer getting her start.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Now, in Chicago you named several fellas that used to sit in with you, white guys. Do you remember Muggsy Spaniel? Oh sure.

Every weekend we'd do breakfast dance there, you know. And a lot of white boys come up there, gangs of them. You know, they used to come in, sit down, blowin' all of them. Limpinico, Louis Primo. All them fellas used to come up there. Louis Primo was very young then though. He was kind of a young kid, you know.
Do you remember Bud Freeman? Sure.
Yes, sure. Where did you know him?
He's from St. Louis, ain't he?
No, he's from Chicago. He played around New York, too.

But I heard he was from St. Louis, Bud Freeman, I know him, played tenor. Mustache. Yeah, I know him, but I heard he was from St. Louis. I don't know where he's from, but I heard that. He's a bad man too, partner.
You know a bass player named Jim Lanagan? Jim Lanagan.
I don't believe, that name sounds familiar, but I don't know him.
What about George Wettland and Davey Tuff, those guys?
I don't know him, white boy. Dave Tuff.
I just wanted to do some of the ones who came around and sat in.

Well, there's so many of them, Dick, I'm telling you, he used to pile in there, man. Of course I tell you what made these to come there, see. Like, take the movie stars like George Ralph, and Harry James, and all them fellas, you know, they'd be in town playing a theater or something, and that breakfast man, they'd be there that morning. And they'd all the people that's come see them, meet them, you know. That's why that happened. Now, I tell you a lady, let's used to be with us, just as regular as we had finger to the toe, and she got to be a big star, Martha Ray.
She'd come to the Golden Leather?

Sure, Martha Ray was dead, it was the regular as that finger to her, get right down that mic and go to singing. She could sing too, partner. And first thing I know, that woman was gone, to California. I said, what's been happening here now? I said, man, they're going into business. Show the real picture. I said, well, I betcha, maybe I know she wouldn't know nothing about me. And I tell you, girl, we started out with us, couldn't sing one song. She gives our name June Richmond now. But her first name is Burdette Richmond. That's her name, Burdette Richmond, because the fella used to sing with us named Ed Goodbar, her mother was his wife. And he brought her up there, brought the girl up there to wake up with us. Said she want to be a song, and we're going to make her learn. And she learned right there with us at the Golden Leather, and got famous right there with us, partner, and hit the road. She first went out with Jimmy Wade. She went on the road with Jimmy Wade. She was a stout girl then, getting started, started. And after Jimmy Wade went back to Chicago and broke up or something like that, next time I heard a boy that, but it was in California.
